title: total war: warhammer
text: Total War Warhammer is an all round great game, but it does have a flaw that prevents it from being a hands down masterpiece. Now even with this flaw I still highly reccomend this game to any fan of dark fantasies and Total War games or RTS's in general. Reasons why you should get this game Include: - A vast amount of rich and interesting lore behind the factions, their characters, individual units and locations to delve into. Warhammer has been around for ages and is an established fantasy IP and with good reason. You'll enjoy the game 100 times more if you learn about all the rivalries and history of the world. - 9 totally unique races/factions to choose from, including ulta violent orcs to manipulative and evil vampire counts. Each faction/race has its individual starting legebdary lords or entirely seperate sub-faction (For example there are the vampire counts and the Von Carsteins who share the same roster but have different starting locations and faction effects) - Every faction/race has their own unique roster, unlike Total War's historic titles no units are reused like spearmen or armored swordsman were where the only difference was a color change, accent and maybe slightly altered stats. Even when two factions have spearmen like the Empire and Brettonia, the spearmen have different models and stats. This makes every unit unique and not like a copy paste - Short battles is a common complaint seen in the reviews of this game. I would say this is a good thing. For instance the reason battles were longer in older titles, for example Medieval 2, is that units were very sturdy and could eat arrow volly after volly and not only that but the animations were slower. This often resulted in periods of battles where all you would do is fast forward because you didn't wanna stare at a slow melee grind for 5 minutes. In more recent titles like Shogun 2 and Warhammer the animations are fluid and quick and units take punishment like they should, thus resulting in quicker battles. Now for the biggest and in my opinion only set back for the game, the price tag. Unfortunatly you sort of need all the dlc to be able to enjoy this game at its fullest. Unfortunatly again, its 60 bucks standard price and with all its dlc you're looking at about 136 dollars, now i bought everything full price and i don't regret that, I think i got my moneys worth but do yourself and favor and pick it up during one of the major sales like the summer or winter sales.

text: If you like Total War games, this might be the mechanically best in the series. The fantasy setting might not be everyone's cup of tea, but the game is very good, with high replayability value. title: train simulator
text: Train Simulator is a constantly-improving simulation of what operating a train is really like. Now that it works again with the "Rail Driver" accessory controller, diesel and electric operation feels a lot more like reality than just pushing buttons on a keyboard or XBox controller. However, these things also work. The positive reviews are correct. Most routes include all the track and visible scenery--buildings, roards, bridges, even seashore--along about 100 miles of track. For example, with the "Pacific Surfliner" DLC, you get everything you would see looking out the windows during the 3 hour ride from San Diego Santa Fe Depot to Los Angeles Union Station. SoCal fans can also choose to purchase the very different experience of Cajon Pass between San Bernadino and Barstow. As others have noted, NONE of the DLC's are necessary to play the original "Train Simulator" game--they don't help you "win" or something like that. Train Simulator DLC's are NOT "PLAY-TO-WIN" like in many other, more competitive, games. All the DLC do is give you more experiences. If all you want to do is run trains on Caltrain to San Francisco or up the North Wales line from Crewe, experinces you can have with the most basic "Train Simulator 2018," you don't have to spend another cent! In addition, "Train Simulator" includes all the tools you need to add or delete track, modify the railroads you buy (or download for free-more on that below), or you can even build an entire new railroad of your own. "TS" also includes the tools you need to make new "schedules," including all the other trains the train you are operating happens to pass. So you can have a lot of fun without spending a penny more after you buy the original game. You can also create your own cars and locomotives, if you have the right graphic tools. I haven't done it, but obviously many others have. One last thing: There are NO good physics if you derail (wreck) your train. That's because this game is about operating trains, not wrecking them. Buy GTA5 if you want a "smash-em up!" If this sounds boring to you: DON'T BUY THIS GAME!  - Respect the people who enjoy it. Now back to "Pacific Surfliner" DLC I live in Oceanside, CA and I travel by rail (and sometimes car) to Los Angeles, San Diego and Orange County often. So I know this line well, and I can recognize many key landmarks the designers incuded. Most of the buildings are generic ones substituting for the real ones, but this game is about trains, not architecture. The Train Simulator version is now "historic," because a lot of new double-track has been laid, and new bridges built, but some TS railroads--like the Pennsylvania R.R. Horseshoe Curve (Altoona-Johnstown) DLC--reproduce a line as it existed fifty years ago, or earlier. How accurate is the "Pacific Surfliner" DLC? Well, I have traveled the Oceanside-San Diego section dozens of times, and driven it along Interstate 5, and I was convinced they just ommitted a few miles between Encinitas and Solana Beach,one of the fastest pieces of track along that segment that includes a town with no station called "Cardiff-on-Sea." I WAS WRONG! There are only four miles between Encinitas and Solana Beach---I checked the Amtrak schedule that lists the mileage--it was just my impression that there was more there. Yes, the designers incuded "Cardiff," but the buildings they used are really generic-looking compared to the riot of color and light at the real place. They also made the San Clemente Pier neighborhood look more blah than it really is. Like I said, this game is about trains and track. For "Pacific Surfliner" DLC, there are two additional for-pay DLC's. One covers the San Diego commuter rail (Coaster), and the other is Los Angeles Orange Co. commuter rail (Metrolink). You get the trains, all painted up accurately, correct locomoties, plus several realistic scenarios that include the Amtrak trains from the "Pacific Surfliner" DLC railroad, along with the Coaster or Metrolink trains you get in these DLC's. Note that, although the LA Commuter rail (Metrolink) DLC scenarios have no San Diego commuter (NCTD Coaster) trains, and vice-versa, now that I own both, I COULD create scenarios that include both Metrolink and Coaster trains. There wouldn't be too much point, except that Coaster and Metrolnk share the same maintenace and storage yard north of Oceanside. The "Pacific Surfliner" DLC includes the entire facility, and it always contains both Coaster and Metrolink trains side by side--plus both railroads run their trains up to their joint yard after dropping off their last passengers of the day at Oceanside. As a result, for several miles of track, you can see Amtrak, Metrolink, Coaster, and BNSF freight trains running by each other. None of these DLC's are very expensive--$19-$39 or so--and they help make "Pacific Surfliner" run a lot more like the real railroad. However, if you didn't want to pay a penny more, you don't have to spend another cent! Furthermoere, "Train Simulator" has a "Community Workshop" where people have uploaded additonal cars, locomoties, scenarios, and even entire new railroads. Most are FREE. In the case of "Pacific Surflinter," some kind soul has uploaded a FREIGHT (Goods) train package so you can also run freight trains up and down the LA-SD route. Being much heavier and longer than passenger trains, freights respond much differently to acceleration and braking. The LA-SD line includes one significant hill just outside San Diego which is challenging in the game -- AND in real life. Railroaders call it "Sorrento Grade." The designer of the Freebie freight scenario also added more information about the geography, like all the "Control Points" along the track that the "Pacific Surfliner" DLC designers left off. You can add your own geographic data to any scenario you want, thus effectively creating a new scenario, with the tools already in "Train Simulator." BTW, since the LA-SD track is so busy during the day, essentialy all freight trains from Fullerton to San Diego operate only at night. The Workshop DLC scenarios should be night-time. However, that is easy to change. You can change the weather--from California Sunshine--to Seattle Rain Squalls--to a Wyoming Snowstorm--aas well as  the time (with the sun and moon changing naturally from day to dusk to night) on any scenario, almsot at will. The Workshop does get complicated, because someone can upload, say, a new scenario for one of the DLC railroads that requires you to add a few other locomotives and cars you have to search and often pay for. However, this is a hobby. Bottom Line: I love model trains, but I don't have the time or space to build any now. "Train Simulator" gives me an experience that is unlike model railroading, but doesn't cost the thousands of dollars one can eventually plow into a well-detailed model railroad. It provides an experience that is even better than model railroading because I can run my train for hours without coming back to the same place.  ALL ABOARD! P.S.: My biggest criticism: The audio is still not really realistic. Why oh why doesn't the the game say something logical like "Highball Metrolink 608!" instead of "O.K. to Proceed"? Basic railroad talk. Well, "Train Simulator 2018" represents the culmination of almost two decades of work, and things can only get better.

text: It's evident from the reviews of Train Simulator that there is a lot of negativity towards it, some of it is justified, some of it is not, personally I am a big fan and it has become the source of hours passing the time. So first common complaint - "it's boring!" simple answer to that is that driving a train is essentially using a limited number of controls in order to make the train move backwards and forwards, stopping and starting, paying attention to signals, opening and closing doors at platforms and/or emptying payload at freight depots. On Train Simulator most of the trains handle in a completely unique manner and this handling changes dependant on the routes you are driving and the weather conditions, so with regards to being a Simulator which accurately depicts driving a train it is probably as close as you can come to the real thing.  If you want added realism you can always purchase one of the third party "train controllers", beyond this the only further improvement to realism would be to have Virtual Reality to allow hands free cockpit navigation, though with the complexity of the graphics at present you would likely need a super computer if that kind of enhancement were ever to be made. Onto the next common complaint - "graphic quality" My personal computer is based on an AMD FX6300 3.5GHz 6 core CPU, 16gb RAM with a 2GB GeForce GT 610 graphics card, it has taken a while for me to tweak the graphic settings in game to an optimal setting, though on the most part have settled with disabling FXAA filtering and 8 x Anisotropic Filtering running at my monitors maximum resolution of 1366 x 768. With those settings I find that most routes work at a very smooth rate, however you have to bear in mind that different production teams have created the routes so the graphic quality does vary significantly across the different routes, and is also impacted by different weather conditions in game and also by some of the individual train models, I personally tend to find that the German routes in particular are extremely heavy on the graphics and often end up with the frame rate dropping significantly, and with that also comes the appearance that time in the game is slowing down (the real time clock does not advance in real time). Next common complaint - "The DLC's cost too much" A quick look through the reviews and it comes up time and time again, people complain about the cost of the add-on's and the fact that in their eyes the base game doesn't have enough content. So first point of note, with the initial game you typically get around 4 routes and circa 8 - 12 locomotives to drive, the routes vary greatly in terms of their length and number of scenarios, though from the base game alone the scenarios will take you in excess of 50 hours to complete should you decide to play all of them, on the scale of things 50 hours of gameplay for a base game is on the higher side of time taken in order to "complete" the base content, so really the criticism there is completely unfounded. Personally, I first purchased Train Simulator 2015, initially didn't really play it much, most of my time spent playing and expanding the game has been over the last 3 - 4 months, and I'm now at the point where I have over 40 different routes and over 100 different locomotives which has probably cost me a couple of hundred pounds, but I've not paid anything like full price for the DLC's I have purchased. So if you were to purchase every single DLC for this game at full price it would cost you well over £4000, but the whole idea of the DLC marketplace element of this game is to allow you to pick and choose the expansions you want, also added to which, if you look at the time it would take to complete every scenario it would stretch into many thousands of hours so realistically for most people if you did actually own every single DLC it would take you YEARS of regular play to even come close to completing all the scenarios. I have expanded my route and locomotive collection by using 3 different methods with the end result being a tiny fraction of the normal cost of purchasing them, and with all the content I have, the surface has barely been scratched with the time I have already spent playing Train Simulator. So first self explanatory money saving method with the DLC's is to purchase them when they are on sale, at present there are Flash Sales regularly occurring on steam for Train Simulator DLC's, and  most weeks even if there is not a major sale there are usually a handful of them available with significant discounts, so it pays to regularly check on the Steam marketplace for the bargains. Next money saving method is to purchase the various collections and/or premium editions of the game, for example, if you have purchased the base Train Simulator 2017 Standard Edition game, you can purchase the First Class Editions of the game to get the 3 additional routes that come with them, just because they have the TS2017 base game included doesn't stop you from taking advantage of the massive savings to be made on the routes, such are the savings to be had on the First Class versions they are cheaper for the 4 additional routes than the individual cost of 1 of the routes included with them, there are also a number of route collections available for Train Simulator which have a "complete your collection" feature where you get a significant discount purchasing compared to the individual cost of each item in the collection. And then what for me has been the most significant savings on Routes, using marketplaces such as♥♥♥♥♥to purchase the Steam code for older versions of the game, yes it can be done, as I mentioned before, even if you already have the Train Simulator base game, you can purchase different versions and Steam will recognise this and give you the Route's and locomotives from the different versions of the game, so I have personally purchased every Train Simulator 13, 14, 15, 16 & 17, in most instances paying only £2.50 - £5 for each version and getting all the routes that come with them including many of the more expensive routes like London Faversham High Speed, Donner Pass, Munich - Augsburg, Sherman Hill and many others, the savings made equate to in excess of a 95% saving on every one of the routes. And the final common complaint - "there are too many bugs" It can't be denied that there is a massive amount of inconsistency across the DLC's, and the bugs can be extremely frustrating, you will no doubt have already read about the most common of them, many of the routes have sudden changes in the speed limit which have no signposting on the rails or indication on the HUD to let you know about them, in some instances the HUD and signposting are telling you the speed limit is changing to one speed when in reality it is changing to a much lower speed so you get hammered with point deductions when attempting to complete career scenarios.  Other common bugs include locomotives that simply won't go anywhere, and if you do eventually get them moving the first time you stop they have an inexplicable emergency stop which you are seemingly unable to reset. With regards to these bugs, every single game you will buy EVER is ALWAYS going to have some kind of bug, most of the time the developers do absolutely nothing to fix them, there are a lot of the bugged routes which have not been fixed, but the fault with this does not necessarily lay with Dovetail Games, but often lays with the third party developers that created the routes in the first place. If you have looked in detail you will have seen that there are many different organisations involved in the creation of routes and locomotive add-on's for Train Simulator, it is evident that many of the developers are quick to fix bugs, where some others don't ever seem to fix anything, so it's not really fair to blame Dovetail for all the bugs. I could go on, but will conclude, Great Simulator and Highly Recommended

The result is a huge number of possible builds and strategies.

title: transistor
text: First things first: play this game with a controller. Transistor is an (almost entirely linear) action RPG set in the city of Cloudbank, a location that appears to be inside a computer, although the characters are entirely human (that is, they do not refer to themselves as programs a la reboot, but as users). The player controls a character named Red as she battles her way through a major world ending crisis using the titular Transistor, a weapon that appears to be able to absorb the energies of dying users. I should tell you right up front that how you feel about the story is going to be how you feel about transistor, since the exploration is minimal and the gameplay is straightforward. It takes a very slow burn approach, and the central conflict isn't really as important as trying to figure out exactly where - or what - cloudbank is. The particulars are left for the player to infer through hints in the dialogue and in the terminals scattered around the levels the player traverses (though these are never well hidden and it is entirely possible to hit every single one of them on your first playthrough without dilly-dallying through nooks and crannies). I found it incredibly exciting, and odds are if you appreicated the story in games like Half-Life 2 or The Last of Us, you are going to enjoy puzzling through exactly what was going on in this place. As for the gameplay itself, aside from traversing the city (which is as simple as moving the left stick on your controller around) you fight in an isometric environment against digital monsters called "the process," using a variety of skills (which you can either use actively, passively, or as a passive upgrade to another skill) and a pretty cool planning mechanic which lets you unleash devastating combos. The whole thing is simultaneously janky and elegant, and by the time all is said and done, you will be very glad the game was so easy and very sad it wasn't more difficult, since you are always free to be creative but it never really feels like you need to do more than button mash. In general, the combat is a good romp and you'll have fun while you're at it, but it just reeks of wasted potential. Overall, I liked this game a lot, but I wish it had spent another few months in the development cycle padding it up. It certainly feels like a much smaller game than Bastion, and they didn't make up for that with additional polish. Go for it, but not at full price. Edit: A quick note that I did not consider. The music varies between this lovely blend of classic rock and roll, new indie rock, and ambient electronica that will appeal to fans of everything from Mogwai to Katy Perry to Adele. However, from time to time it also indulges in some bluesy garbage that I'm sure was intended to be "soulful," as in the pretentious, pejorative sense. The soundtrack features very prominently, so you should be aware of it.

text: Before we begin, let us establish something that should be obvious from the game's title, but apparently isn't to some players: THIS IS NOT BASTION 2 Playing it like it was Bastion 2 can only lead to frustration and disaappointment. To appreciate Transistor, you must approach it respectfully, on its own terms, and not guided by your own expectations, as, really, you should be doing with every game worth talking about. While it uses some of the same innovative mechanisms that were introduced in Bastion, it is not, nor does it try to be, more of the same - something I admire with Supergiant's production that, apparently, some players of the game find frustration with. They could've easily printed money by making a Bastion 2, but chose to make something original instead. How can you not admire such a departure from the unscrupulous money grab that is sadly becoming the norm in this hobby? I've likely already gifted you this game if we're on reasonably friendly terms. But for everyone else, allow me to say that, speaking as an experienced gamer, this is my favourite game. It is, in a word, perfection, and those of you who know how critical I can be of these things should know I do not say that lightly. Perfectly harmonized design, art direction, music, writing, everything. The team at Supergiant, earning themselves a place as my personal favourite developers, and in any case an honoured spot on the true A-list, have here created another superbly crafted game that I warmly encourage everyone to try and experience.

text: This game has a beautiful and unique way of storytelling. The story doesn't fit into any specific genre, and is confusing in a good way, meaning you can't predict it based on other stories/games. The art style fits perfectly and the soundtrack is just beautiful and well integrated into the gameplay. Yet the biggest surprise for me is the gameplay and skill system. The way of combining functions (skills) allows for many different effective play styles without forcing the player into making permanent choices. It doesn't make much sense to compare Transistor and Bastion, since their concepts are quite different. I personally liked Transistor better, since it's art style and gameplay goes even further away from a usual fantasy setting.

text: 剧情简单来讲就是红发黑丝萌妹与一支大宝剑的虐狗故事。与前作不同的赛博朋客和相同的 的灭世设定，结局非常感人： ，为什么呢？Transistor, transits the world. 战斗方面非常有新意，即时+回合策略合理运用可以事半功倍。节奏比较适中，上手了速通三小时也可以完成。 技能方面非常有新意，大宝剑可以吸收各种NPC的意识（灵魂），每个灵魂可以分别作为主动技手动释放，或者被动技与其它意识组合出新效果，亦或者作为属性技能直接装备。 画面的话光影和色彩的运用更好了，和前作不同这次基色调偏冷，并更多地使用了3D效果。。相同的是依然可以随手截图就是一张壁纸~哈哈。高潮部分和结局的手绘CG配合剧情效果很震撼。 音乐保持了Supergiant Games一贯的高水准，空灵优雅，很符合主角失声歌手的气质和灾难过后空城里忧伤的氛围，个人觉得比Bastion更加好，推荐入OST。 总之独立游戏这是第一个能让我二周目的作品，期待今年发布的第三部新作。 Gameplay: 9/10 Control: 8.5/10 Story: 11/10 Salute! Music: 10/10 Graphic: 9/10 10/10 Would be Penetra-nsis-ted again lol. 刚才翻了下YouTube有关这游戏结局的评论，发现不少人不喜欢这个ending,前作是有两个不同的结局可以选择的，而这作只有一个结局。然而多了一个细思恐极的看似是NG+的mode。个人觉得，这是制作组对在前作自己抛出的问题 给出的一个明确的答案。
